core: Earth systems, climate and landscape change
Land use, ecosystems and sustainable food systems
Economics, public decisions and environmental value
Field, geospatial, statistical and interdisciplinary research methods
adjacent: Flood risk, water scarcity and nature-based adaptation
Energy transition, resource scarcity and circular response
questions: How can earth observation and field evidence guide flood adaptation?
How should scarce resources be managed across markets, policy and environmental systems?

trace: Introduces physical and quantitative principles used to examine sustainability systems.
Studies interacting lithosphere and hydrosphere processes through Earth science and field labs.
Introduces incentives, markets and scarcity for evaluating environmental choices.
Studies waves,chemistry andmaterialscience applied tosustainability, withreflectivejournals/greenwashingproject; foundation foradvancedresourcecourses,not a genericproject substitute.
Introduces quantitative research design and statistics for economic or environmental evidence.
Analyses natural hazards, exposure, climate-driven risks and adaptation measures.
Teaches calculus,integration,complexnumbers anddifferentialequations in appliedprojects; not assumed to cover every VU mathematicaltopic.
Examines climate drivers, impacts and adaptation, including sea-level rise.
Studies nature-based infrastructure across coasts, rivers, cities and ports, using ecological-corridor and intervention-design projects.

Studies organism diversity, classification and ecological roles using identification, biodiversity indices and a small phylogenetic/data project; it provides biological foundations rather than a full conservation-management course.
Works with and visualises spatial datasets as evidence for interdisciplinary inquiry.
Applies ArcGIS Pro georeferencing, projections, queries and surface analysis plus remote-sensing preprocessing/image processing to a collaborative environmental case study.
Studies soils and aquifers with field and laboratory analysis relevant to water resources and coastal defence.
Analyses choice under scarcity and regulation, grounding economic evaluation of resource use.
Studies flood, sea-level and subsidence adaptation through delta water-management projects.

Studies aqueous composition, speciation, redox, adsorption and weathering with geochemical modelling and laboratory investigations. Dynamic Earth and Soils & Aquifers precede it; formal prerequisite Sustainability Essentials I is met.
Examines circular-economy recovery technologies, material stewardship and resource security.
Provides probability and statistical inference for quantitative environmental evidence.
Researches geoscience of geothermal energy, waste storage and carbon capture.
Evaluates how government and non-government stakeholders shape sustainability policy.
Develops causal and predictive empirical analysis of economic data; environmental application is a possible project, not course-specific.
Studies public goods, externalities, taxation and welfare effects of policy, applicable to environmental decisions.
Designs lower-carbon energy systems with technical and economic assessment.
Studies aggregate output,growth,inflation,trade andfiscal/monetarypolicy; broad economic context,not a dedicatedenergytransition course.

Applies spatial engineering, GIS and remote-sensing methods to disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring through hands-on projects; specific techniques beyond the description are not assumed.
Quantifies renewable resources, conversion and storage; applies Polysun modelling, hydropower sizing, experiments and mini-grid analysis to energy options.
Compares environmental, social, health and economic consequences across product/process life cycles, including costs and revenues; staged projects culminate in an integrated life-cycle assessment.
Develops structured and object-oriented Python programming, testing and debugging as the implementation foundation for computational environmental inquiry.
Studies algorithm design, data structures, complexity and experimental benchmarking; general computational reasoning complements physical/spatial analysis, not a guaranteed environmental project.

Applies regression/classification, resampling, regularisation, trees, support-vector and unsupervised methods to real data; general predictive/inferential tools complement GIS/environmental evidence without promising project topics.

Builds neural networks in Python/Keras/TensorFlow, including backpropagation, regularisation and image/time-series/text prediction; environmental applications are compositional, not assumed classroom examples.

Studies interactingEarthspheres,systemmodelling,proxies andisotopetracers forpast/futureclimate with a greenhouse-gas-pathwaysfieldtrip; description-only evidence considered fully within stated scope.

alternatives.label: Earth systems, economics and sustainable development
alternatives.concept: Combine Earth and climate science, soils, water and biodiversity with economics, quantitative methods and sustainability governance. Geological and laboratory fieldwork, GIS and spatial projects connect physical evidence with adaptation and energy decisions; dedicated environmental economics, advanced sustainability data science and the individual VU thesis remain important gaps.
alternatives.labelReason: The schedule spans Earth science, water, climate, resources, economics, spatial data and policy; the title describes its actual interdisciplinary core.
progression: Current2026h2–2029h1offerings andallformalprerequisites checked. GateI precedesGateII,EarthObservation andenvironmental/energydependents;GateIIprecedesSpatialPlanning,R3andResources;DynamicEarth/Soils precedeadvancedbiogeochemistry. Methods/statistics precede economicapplications; calculus precedesProbability. Actualfield/geospatial/labfoundations precede advanced resourceanalysis; spatialengineering andEarthObservation runconcurrently with no additionalhardprerequisite invented.

alternatives.label: Resources, energy and economic evaluation
alternatives.concept: Connect Earth-resource science with energy-system analysis, renewable design, resource recovery and life-cycle assessment. Five economics courses add 37.5 EC of theory, public-policy analysis and econometrics, giving this direction greater economic and technical energy weight than the integrated water, risk and biodiversity programme.
alternatives.labelReason: Actual resource,energy-conversion/design,life-cycle,circular-recovery andfiveeconomiccourses substantiate the title; generic economics is not renamed a specialist environmental-economics course.
progression: Current2026h2–2029h1offerings andallformalprerequisites checked. GateI precedesGateII,EarthObservation andenvironmental/energydependents;GateIIprecedesSpatialPlanning,R3andResources;DynamicEarth/Soils precedeadvancedbiogeochemistry. Methods/statistics precede economicapplications; calculus precedesProbability. Actualfield/geospatial/labfoundations precede advanced resourceanalysis; spatialengineering andEarthObservation runconcurrently with no additionalhardprerequisite invented.
alternatives.distinctness: Four courses (30 EC) differ in each direction. The integrated programme emphasises hazards, nature-based infrastructure, biodiversity and delta water management. This direction instead adds macroeconomics, public economics, life-cycle assessment and renewable-system design. All differences are substantive consequences of economic evaluation and resource/energy focus, not numerical substitutions.

alternatives.label: Environmental modelling, spatial data and machine learning
alternatives.concept: Combine Earth systems, water and delta systems, geospatial analysis and physical environmental investigation with programming, algorithms, machine learning and neural prediction. The computational courses supply general methods for environmental questions supported by the science courses; particular environmental project topics are not guaranteed, and specialist environmental economics, ethics and the VU thesis remain gaps.
alternatives.labelReason: SubstantialEarth/water/field/GISstudy plus generalprogramming,algorithms,statisticallearning andneuralnetworkmodels implements the explicitlyevidencedenvironmentalAI/data direction. No dedicated environmentalAIcourse orproject guarantee claimed.
progression: Current2026h2–2029h1offerings andallformalprerequisites checked. GateI precedesGateII,EarthObservation andenvironmental/energydependents;GateIIprecedesSpatialPlanning,R3andResources;DynamicEarth/Soils precedeadvancedbiogeochemistry. Methods/statistics precede economicapplications; calculus precedesProbability. Programming in secondautumn precedesalgorithms,ML andneuralwork. Priorresearchstatistics supplies ML preparation;Probability/ML/algorithms inthirdautumnprecedeNeuralNetworks in finalspring. EarthSystemTools followsGateI in firstspring.
alternatives.distinctness: Five courses (37.5 EC) differ from the closest and seven (52.5 EC) from the resource/economic programme. Programming, algorithms, machine learning, neural networks and Earth-system modelling replace biodiversity, nature-based infrastructure, renewable-energy analysis, microeconomics and governance relative to the closest. These choices shift the organising priority to computational environmental inquiry, not cosmetic substitutions.

routeSelection.basis: The standard full-time bachelor has no formal specialisation to select. Its third-year restricted choice is 6 EC from Stedelijke uitdagingen or a 6-EC thesis extension; the first-listed urban course is selected in source order without reference to UCR fit. The 30-EC genuinely open minor space is not treated as compulsory geography coursework.

selection.assessment: Three substantive completeprogrammes pass after reassessing the currentcoursepool. Resource/energy/economic directionpassesfirst, withlife-cyclecost/environmentalassessment and5economicscourses. Thenenvironmentalmodelling/data/AI passes: actualEarth/water/GIS/fieldscience withprogramming,algorithms,MLandneuralprediction has5courses37.5ECdifferentfromclosest and7courses52.5ECfromeconomicoption. Thesearenewacademicpriorities, not4arbitraryfloor substitutions. Explicitrow69AI interest is implemented throughgeneralcomputationalmethods combinedwithenvironmentalscience,without guaranteedprojecttopics. No furtherprogramme beyond authorisedmaximum3.

notes.text: These UCR programmes combine substantial Earth and sustainability study with different economic or computational priorities. They do not reproduce dedicated environmental economics, physical hydrology and nature-management depth, environmental ethics, VU’s two specified fieldwork units or its required individual 12-EC thesis. Data and machine-learning courses supply general methods alongside environmental science, rather than the same sustainability Big Data course. Optional independent research requires approval and is outside the 24-course schedules; it does not replace the VU thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Earth Sciences, Economics and Sustainability connects physical Earth systems with economic choices and spatial sustainability problems. Students study climate risk, water, land, energy and resources using field research, data analysis and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers an integrated Earth, water, risk and biodiversity programme, a resource and energy programme with greater economic evaluation, and a computational direction combining environmental science with programming and machine learning. Spatial analysis, laboratory and field activities support these related responses. Dedicated environmental economics, advanced sustainability-specific data science, environmental ethics, VU’s specified fieldwork and the individual thesis remain important differences. Computational courses provide general methods; particular environmental project topics are not guaranteed.

curriculum.routeLabel: Ordinary full-time bachelor; Urban Challenges restricted elective
curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC comprises 144 EC of required courses, one 6 EC restricted choice and 30 EC of free study. Fieldwork preparation requires 24 eligible first-year EC; second-year fieldwork requires 60 EC including the first fieldwork. Thesis entry requires 126 EC including recognised fieldwork. Free-choice courses have level and approval rules. The first-year study-advice norm is 42 EC. A language test or remediation gates the Soil and Landscape grade; mentoring and Geoflex obligations carry no credits.
